newsitem.title: TURKEY: SOCCER SHOWCASE-FIRE AND ICE AS SUKUR FACES BOLIC.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER SHOWCASE-FIRE AND ICE AS SUKUR FACES BOLIC.

text.p: Sunday's first division derby in Istanbul could provide a fire and ice scenario as Fenerbahce and Galatasaray look to the two highest scorers in the Turkish league to tip the balance.
Elvir Bolic and Hakan Sukur, whose teams face each other across the narrow Bosphorus strait that divides Europe and Asia through Istanbul, also share many similarities.
Born within a month of each other, both men are Moslems, both have worn the Galatasaray colours and both have a fierce hunger for goals.
But in terms of temperament, they, too, might as well be continents apart.

In Sukur, Galatasaray have the fire of a moody but brilliant goalscorer who is currently the leading marksman in Turkey with 20 goals. Fenerbahce, on the other hand, have the icy cool temperament of Bolic who now has 14 goals to his name this season.
Bolic began his career in the small town of Zenica, Bosnia, where he was born in 1971, before graduating to Red Star Belgrade, the top team of the then unified Yugoslavia.

As a Bosnian Moslem, Bolic left Belgrade as the war raged in 1992 and headed for the old Ottoman capital of Istanbul where he signed for Galatasaray. He played half a season, scored three goals and was prompty loaned to lowly Gaziantepspor in Turkey's troubled southeast in 1993.
Meanwhile, Big Hakan, as he is known to the fans, also began his career by playing for his local side Sakaryaspor before being sold to Bursaspor.

A move to Galatasaray followed in 1990 and Sukur was an immediate hit with the supporters, impressing everyone with his darting runs and ability to steal vital goals as in Galatasaray's 2-1 defeat of Barcelona in November 1994.
Galatasaray saw the opportunity for Sukur to tread a bigger stage and collected a reported 2.5 million German marks ($1.5 million) by selling him to Torino at the end of the season.

It took an audience with doleful Moslem cleric Fethullah Gulen, leader of a religious sect, to persuade Sukur to go to Italy but he never settled. He was homesick -- he said he missed kebabs -- and lovesick.
he result was a quick trip back to Turkey where he married his girlfriend, a university student, and brought her back to Italy.
Unfortunately, this new domestic situation did not work for him either. Press reports at the time said that he wanted meals ready on the table after the match but his wife was too busy studying.
Sukur made just five appearances for Torino and scored one goal before the Italians washed their hands of him and he returned to Galatasaray for an estimated 1.8 million marks.
"Torino can do without his contribution. We prefer to concentrate on players who cost less and give more," Torino sporting director Giorgio Vitali said at the time.

Bolic, in the meantime, made the best of his two-year exile with humble Gaziantepspor, who had bought him for some 400,000 marks. He scored 11 goals for them in the 1994-95 season, prompting Fenerbahce to sign him for twice that fee.
Since then the pair have flourished on the field. In the 1995-96 season they became their clubs' top scorers, Bolic hitting 22 and Sukur 16.
Bolic has remained the cool professional, unphased by adversity and impeccable on the pitch.

And he is still scoring goals. In one memorable week at the end of last year he broke Manchester United's 40-year unbeaten record in Europe at Old Trafford and then gave Bosnia their first win on home soil in Sarajevo with the winner in their 2-1 defeat of Italy.

Not quite the same can be said about Hakan who first refused to talk to the press when he returned from Italy and then made the wrong kind of headlines when, after returning goalless from Euro '96, he was allegedly involved in a fracas with some youngsters who pointed out his failure to score.
The Turks, though, clearly love Big Hakan as one of their own. He's sometimes misguided, over-emotional and prone to being too sensitive but he's a fighter and, ultimately, a winner.
